claims.claim: Labor (total compensation and related expenses) is the single largest category of hospital operating expense, accounting for about 56% of total hospital costs in the AHA's 2025 Cost of Caring report.

In Aiken et al.'s 2002 JAMA study of 168 Pennsylvania hospitals (10,184 nurses; 232,342 surgical patients), each additional patient per nurse was associated with a 7% increase in the odds of 30-day mortality (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.03-1.12) and a 7% increase in failure-to-rescue (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.02-1.11); higher ratios also raised nurse burnout (OR 1.23) and job dissatisfaction (OR 1.15).

California was the first U.S. state to enact minimum licensed nurse-to-patient ratios (Assembly Bill 394, 1999); implementing regulations took effect January 1, 2004, setting, for example, a 1-nurse-to-5-patient ratio on medical-surgical units. Whether such mandates improve outcomes is debated, and there is no single universal national ratio standard.

One full-time equivalent (1.0 FTE) conventionally represents 2,080 paid hours per year (40 hours x 52 weeks); hours per patient day (HPPD/NHPPD) divides the productive nursing hours worked in 24 hours by the patient census and is a standard productivity and budgeting measure.

In the 2026 NSI National Health Care Retention & RN Staffing Report (527 hospitals; calendar-year 2025 data), the average staff-RN turnover rate was 17.6% (up from 16.4% in 2024), the average cost of turnover for one bedside RN was $60,090, and the average hospital lost between $4.2 million and $6.2 million; each one-percentage-point change in RN turnover was worth about $295,000 per year to the average hospital.

Registered nurses are the largest clinical profession, holding about 3,391,000 jobs in 2024, which makes nurse staffing the dominant driver of hospital labor budgets; medical and health services managers (about 616,200 jobs in 2024) plan and direct this workforce.

Skill mix (the proportion of RNs to LPNs, aides, and other staff) and scope-appropriate assignment let organizations match staff qualifications to the acuity of the work, which is central to controlling labor cost while maintaining safe care.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether mandated minimum nurse-to-patient ratios improve patient outcomes and are the right policy tool.
positions: Observational studies (e.g., Aiken et al.) associate richer nurse staffing with lower mortality and failure-to-rescue, supporting minimum-staffing arguments.

Critics note that mandated fixed ratios can be costly, may not account for patient acuity or unit context, and that the causal effect of California's ratios on outcomes has been mixed in later evaluations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the association evidence and attributes it carefully to specific studies, states that California enacted the first mandated ratios, and explicitly notes the debate rather than asserting a settled universal standard.

sourceRecords.title: Hospital Nurse Staffing and Patient Mortality, Nurse Burnout, and Job Dissatisfaction (Aiken, Clarke, Sloane, Sochalski, Silber, 2002)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the association between patient-to-nurse ratio and outcomes: each additional patient per nurse OR 1.07 (95% CI 1.03-1.12) for 30-day mortality and OR 1.07 (1.02-1.11) for failure-to-rescue; burnout OR 1.23; dissatisfaction OR 1.15; 168 PA hospitals, 10,184 nurses, 232,342 surgical patients. PubMed abstract page required cookies for the fetcher; verified the numeric results via the Europe PMC REST API (EXT_ID:12387650). Canonical PubMed URL registered.

sourceRecords.title: Assembly Bill 394 (1999) — Health facilities: nursing staff (California minimum nurse-to-patient ratios)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports that AB 394 (1999) directed California's Department of Health Services to set minimum, specific, numerical licensed nurse-to-patient ratios by classification and unit — the first such state law. Implementing regulations took effect January 1, 2004 (e.g., 1:5 on medical-surgical units, phased from 1:6). Bill text read from the California Legislative Information site; implementation timeline corroborated by CHCF/CGA secondary summaries.

sourceRecords.title: 2026 NSI National Health Care Retention & RN Staffing Report
sourceRecords.notes: Supports CY2025 workforce metrics from 527 participating hospitals: staff-RN turnover 17.6% (up from 16.4% in CY2024), overall hospital turnover 18.5%, RN vacancy 8.6%, average cost of turnover for one bedside RN $60,090, average hospital loss $4.2M-$6.2M, and $295,000 per year per one-point change in RN turnover; hospitals lost $5.19M on average in 2025. Verified by decompressing the PDF's Flate streams locally (WebFetch returned only binary); figures cross-checked against Becker's Hospital Review summary.

sourceRecords.title: Hours per patient day: Understanding this key measure of productivity
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definitions of hours per patient day (HPPD/NHPPD) as total productive nursing hours in 24 hours divided by census, the distinction between productive and nonproductive hours, that there is no single standard HPPD calculation, and its use as a budgeting/productivity measure. FTE = 2,080 paid hours/year corroborated by the ScienceDirect article 'Understanding FTEs and Nursing Hours Per Patient Day.'
